subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I'm planning the scale and proportions for a stylized keel-billed toucan model with its distinctive long beak, positioning it perched on a mossy branch with an orchid, aiming for realistic size proportions around 50-55 cm.

I'm working out the layout so the branch rests naturally at ground level, with the bird facing forward and gripping the perch, making sure the lowest points of the model touch the floor plane convincingly.

I'll design a simple mossy mound base sitting on the ground, with the branch angling up from it so the bird has a readable perch, and I need to carefully set the sphere's vertical scale so it doesn't sink unrealistically into the floor.

Let me simplify further into a mossy stump shape — a tapered cylinder with a moss cap sphere on top — and have the branch rest on that stump instead.

Now I'm placing a toucan on top of the branch, sizing it against real keel-billed toucan proportions: roughly 0.3m body plus tail, and a 0.2m beak extending forward, angled upright like a typical perched pose, with the bird group origin set at its feet gripping the branch.

I'm setting up the local body frame with torso, head, and tail positions, then planning to rotate the whole group around the X axis so the upright head leans forward toward +Z while the tail dips down-back, working through the rotation math to get the tilt direction right.

Since feet need to sit at the branch top, I'm thinking through how the torso's bottom point shifts after rotation, aiming to construct the feet positions directly in the already-tilted frame rather than fighting the rotation offsets afterward.

Thinking about whether to rotate the whole group around the feet pivot versus rotating individual body parts for finer control — rotating the group tilts legs and body together like a leaning bird, which seems visually plausible for a perched pose, but individually rotating parts like the torso ellipsoid might give cleaner results, so I'm leaning toward that approach.

I'm working out the upright coordinate frame for the bird with feet at the origin, defining torso dimensions as a compact ellipsoid and figuring out where the head and toes sit before applying the overall tilt.

The toucan's feet are zygodactyl, with two toes pointing forward and two back, colored bright blue and wrapping over the branch, while the legs consist of short tarsus cylinders with the thighs hidden under body feathers. I'm placing the glossy black torso as an ellipsoid and adding a lemon-yellow bib ellipsoid patch on the front chest to mimic the toucan's throat coloring.

Now I'm positioning a scarlet undertail patch and shaping the black tail as a thin, angled box pitched downward and back from the torso base to match the bird's natural posture.

This angle math is getting messy, so I should switch to a cleaner approach: a generic helper that orients a tapered cylinder between two points using quaternion alignment, avoiding manual rotation angle calculations for each limb or tail segment.

Now I'm thinking through the toucan beak shape—large, long, deep, tapered with a slight downward curve at the tip—and planning the color layout from base to tip: lime green, sky blue, orange, ending in a cherry-red tip.

I'll build the beak along a curving spine, stacking tapered elliptical segments to match the real keel-billed toucan's laterally compressed, deep shape, with each colored band as its own mesh segment.

I'm also adding a small dark nostril notch and a black gape line for detail. For the beak placement, I'm plotting a spine curve from the head front, angling slightly downward and forward to a tip roughly 0.2m away, accounting for the head's forward tilt in world space.

The beak needs to be proportionally huge, close to the length of the body itself, so I'm curving it downward toward the tip using a quadratic bezier for that characteristic keel-billed shape. I'm breaking the beak into 16 segments along the curve, each built from a scaled cylinder oriented along the tangent direction, with width and height tapering appropriately to get the elliptical cross-section right.

So in the cylinder's local space, the X axis maps to width and Z maps to height, since side×T works out to roughly the vertical direction when T points forward. I'll build the rotation matrix from these basis vectors and derive the quaternion from it, then set the mesh's scale to halfWidth and halfHeight accordingly before positioning it.

For tapering smoothly between segments rather than looking stepped, I realize non-uniform scaling can't vary radius independently at each end of a cylinder, so I'll need to construct the beak as a custom lofted geometry instead — generating rings of points along the spine, each shaped into an ellipse, connecting them with faces, capping the tip, and assigning colors per band through separate geometries or groups.

Defining ring points and taper profile...

I'm closing the base and tip with cap vertices so the loft seals cleanly against the head sphere, then dividing the beak's length into colored bands — green near the base transitioning through blue, orange, and red at the tip — to mimic a keel-billed toucan's rainbow pattern.

I'm considering simplifying by keeping band boundaries straight across the loft rather than jagged, and adding small detail touches like a dark nostril ellipsoid near the base rather than a full gape line, to avoid overcomplicating the geometry.

The tiny open hole at the tip would be invisible at this scale, but I'll add a center vertex and fan triangles there anyway, keeping the base hidden inside the head sphere. I'm now writing the loft code itself, generating rings across four material bands with vertex positions and indices, then will compute vertex normals on the indexed geometry.

Writing ring generation loop...

I fix the up-vector by computing it as tangent crossed with side instead, confirming it points upward correctly. Then I build each ring's vertices using side and up vectors scaled by width and height, with an asymmetry so the lower mandible half is shorter than the upper half to match the toucan's beak shape. Now I'm setting up the triangle indexing scheme connecting adjacent rings around the beak's circumference.

Working out the triangle winding so normals face outward, confirming the pattern holds for both quad triangles and the tip fan where the last ring collapses to a point at the spine's end.

I'm checking that the beak base ring sits inside the head sphere so the geometry joins cleanly without gaps. Then I'm settling on vertex counts and the material setup — four colored bands (lime, sky blue, orange, cherry-red tip) mapped via a material array — and starting to think through the toucan's head coloring, recalling that keel-billed toucans actually have mostly black heads and bodies with the colorful bill.

Now I'm pinning down the color palette: glossy black for the body, lemon-yellow for the throat bib, lime-green for the bare eye-ring skin, bright blue feet, and scarlet undertail coverts, alongside the beak's lime/sky-blue/orange/red bands. I'm also planning the eye as a dark sphere with a small white glint inside the lime ring, plus branch bark in brown, mossy green clumps, and a pink orchid accent.

I'm deciding to skip canvas-based textures for robustness and stick with simple colored primitives instead, then I'm moving on to work out the head and eye-ring geometry placement.

Actually I should use a torus ring around a black eye sphere, oriented with its axis along X so it faces outward on the side of the head, with the black eye sphere nested slightly inside the lime ring. For the throat bib, I'm positioning a yellow pear-shaped ellipsoid beneath the beak, overlapping the lower-front area of the head sphere just enough to look tucked under it without poking through awkwardly—checking the z and y coordinates against the head sphere's surface to confirm the bib reads as separate from the head but close beneath the beak's base.

Now I'm working out the torso placement relative to the head and legs, setting the torso as a larger ellipsoid whose top meets the head's bottom to form a continuous body silhouette, then figuring out how the short tarsus/leg segments bridge the gap between the torso's underside and the feet, likely using thin grey cylindrical segments from hip to ankle.

I'm deciding feet and legs should both be the bright blue color, then working out toe placement so toes appear to wrap over the top of the branch cylinder, accounting for the branch's curvature so the toes sit naturally on its surface rather than floating above or sinking into it.

Actually, if I place the body group's position at the pivot point and define children relative to that pivot by subtracting it from their absolute coordinates, rotation will correctly pivot around the hip rather than the world origin. If I instead rotated about the world origin at foot level, the whole body would swing forward unrealistically, changing its height and position — so I need the pivot-relative approach to keep the stance grounded correctly.

Working through the tail geometry under the lean rotation, I'm computing the base and tip positions relative to the hip pivot and transforming them by the 30° lean to find their world coordinates, checking the resulting length and angle look plausible for a toucan's tail before deciding whether the overall body lean is too extreme.

Now I'm projecting the head position through the same rotation to confirm the forward-lean pose makes sense, then stacking up the overall height budget — stump, branch, bird body, head — against real toucan proportions to sanity-check the model's total scale. I'm settling on a layered world layout starting from ground level: a mossy stump base, then the branch resting on it, then the perched bird.

Next I'm placing the stump at the origin with its top around y≈0.22, and setting the horizontal branch above it along the Z-axis so its bottom edge rests flush on the stump top, giving the branch top surface at roughly y=0.28. Then I'm working out where the bird's feet should sit on that branch surface, nudging the bird slightly forward along Z, and checking that the toe geometry lands just above the branch top as expected — while also starting to think through how the bird's lengthwise body orientation relates to standing crosswise on a perch like real birds do.

I'll place the orchid on the branch at x≈0.25, slightly right of the bird, with its stem rising sideways into blossoms, while keeping the bird at x=-0.1 and stump at x=0 for balance. For the branch itself I'm building it from tapered cylinder segments with a slight kink partway along, using small spheres at the joints to hide the seams, plus a broken stub at the left end for a natural branchy look.

Now I'm sketching the mossy stump base: a tapered cylinder sized so its top meets the branch bottom exactly, topped with a flattened moss cap and scattered jittered green blobs along the sides, all sitting on a flattened dodecahedron rock whose bottom I'm aligning to y=0 by checking its vertex geometry.

I'll write a helper that auto-grounds any mesh by computing its world bounding box and shifting it so the lowest point sits at y=0, which simplifies placing irregularly-shaped boulders without manual math. For the rock-and-stump composition, I'm planning a boulder stretched wide and flattened, topped with a short wooden stump jutting up to meet the branch.

Working through the vertical stack: stump top at ~0.22, branch center at 0.25 so its top sits near 0.28, and the bird's feet rest there. Stacking up the bird's leaning posture and head puts the total model height around 0.68-0.7m, a bit larger than a real toucan but acceptable since the design calls for a stylized oversized head and beak.

For the body I'm sizing the torso at roughly 0.21m tall with a 0.15m head, which fits a real keel-billed toucan's proportions once the exaggerated beak is added. I'm dialing back the perch lean from 30° to 22° for a more natural upright stance with the tail hanging down.

Now I'm designing the orchid: a thin green stalk rising from the branch with several phalaenopsis-style blooms, each built from radially arranged pink petal ellipsoids, a magenta lip, and a small yellow column sphere, with multiple blossoms along one arching stem counting as a single orchid plant.

Placing the orchid beside the bird on the branch, with a mossy base and an arching stalk curving upward through several points toward smaller blooms at the top, each flower's five petals positioned and rotated radially around its center so they fan outward in a plane facing roughly toward the camera.

For moss, I'll scatter flattened low-poly icosahedron blobs along the branch top in two shades of green with slight random jitter, applying flat shading for that faceted, stylized look.
